title: The Man Behind a West Bank Telegram Channel Trying to Keep Palestinian Drivers Safe
gist: Anas Hattab's volunteer-run 'Road Conditions' Telegram group, with nearly 350,000 followers, has become the de facto real-time checkpoint-status utility for Palestinians in the West Bank because mainstream navigation apps ignore 942 barriers. WIRED's reporting used its data to show checkpoint delays up over 50 percent since October 2023, while the operation depends on unpaid moderators and one exhausted founder.

insights.claim: Major navigation apps such as Google Maps do not mark the 942 checkpoints, gates and other barriers fragmenting the West Bank and default to algorithmically fastest routes that often run through settlements and Israeli-controlled areas.
insights.speaker: Lama Rabah
insights.so_what: Mainstream mapping products have a structural blind spot in contested territories, leaving room for local data utilities.

insights.claim: Israel restricts or bars Palestinian vehicles from many main West Bank arteries while Israeli vehicles pass freely, so a Palestinian driver following app directions risks arrest, fines or being shot.
insights.speaker: Lama Rabah
insights.so_what: The failure is a safety issue, not just a convenience gap, which raises the value of verified local data.

insights.claim: Trips that used to take Hattab one hour from Tulkarm to Ramallah now often take two to three hours or far longer because of military checkpoints.
insights.speaker: Lama Rabah
insights.so_what: Illustrates the daily cost of the checkpoint regime on mobility.

insights.claim: Hattab launched the Telegram group 'Road Conditions' in 2019 so Palestinians could share checkpoint delays, closures and settler or military presence; membership came as a trickle at first and a flood once checkpoints multiplied in 2022.
insights.speaker: Lama Rabah
insights.so_what: A simple chat group scaled into critical infrastructure because it filled an information void.

insights.claim: Nearly 350,000 people follow the group, local radio stations build their hourly road segments from its dispatches, and a routing system used by West Bank companies plus a new local app ingest its data.
insights.speaker: Lama Rabah
insights.so_what: Downstream products depend on a single volunteer-run data source, which is both a moat and a fragility.

insights.claim: To keep reports reliable, Hattab closed the public chat and recruited active contributors as moderators; more than a dozen volunteers verify each report by asking people on the ground, cross-checking local pages or driving the roads themselves before anything is posted.
insights.speaker: Lama Rabah
insights.so_what: Human verification plus restricted posting is the quality mechanism for crowdsourced real-time data.

insights.claim: Status in the feed changes within minutes ('clear', 'open' and 'closed' can all be true within the same hour), and user spikes of thousands at a time during city lockdowns generate thousands of questions a day for the founder.
insights.speaker: Lama Rabah
insights.so_what: Real-time accuracy requirements make this a labor-intensive service that is hard to automate.

insights.claim: Hattab's odometer went from 70,000 to 274,000 kilometers in four years inside a territory about 130 kilometers across, and he spent six months driving without a destination to learn every checkpoint name and bypass route.
insights.speaker: Lama Rabah
insights.so_what: Ground-truth knowledge, not technology, is the scarce input in this system.

insights.claim: An investigation published in September with the Palestine Reporting Lab, Arab Reporters for Investigative Journalism and Lighthouse Reports found checkpoint delays up more than 50 percent since October 7, 2023.
insights.speaker: Lama Rabah
insights.so_what: Provides a quantified baseline for the deterioration of West Bank mobility.

insights.claim: The average West Bank commuter now loses about 77 hours a year on roundabout routes to avoid checkpoints, and formerly 10-minute drives between towns have become hour-long trips.
insights.speaker: Lama Rabah
insights.so_what: Time lost translates into an economic drag on the territory.

insights.claim: No official data exists on checkpoint delays, so WIRED's team built its database by scraping updates that originated in Hattab's Road Conditions group.
insights.speaker: Lama Rabah
insights.so_what: Crowdsourced channels can be the only available dataset in opaque conflict settings.

insights.claim: After October 2023 a soldier near Qalqilya took Hattab's phone, scrolled through about 20,000 photos he had received, and ordered him to delete everything; he deleted thousands before being released, and now avoids showing military jeeps or any soldier in posts.
insights.speaker: Lama Rabah
insights.so_what: Operators of such channels face device searches and self-censor, which limits the information they can publish.

insights.claim: Settlers in nearly 150 official settlements and 185 new outposts established since 2023 have become a daily threat; the Colonization and Wall Resistance Commission documented nearly 5,443 settler attacks in 2025 and about 4,766 in the first eight months of 2026.
insights.speaker: Lama Rabah
insights.so_what: Settler violence is running at a pace similar to or above 2025 levels, raising demand for real-time warnings.

insights.claim: Hattab can predict follow-on closures across a whole corridor when a major junction shuts, 'like dominoes'.
insights.speaker: Lama Rabah
insights.so_what: Experience-based pattern recognition adds predictive value beyond raw reporting.

insights.claim: Hattab runs the operation with no institutional support and two young children, cannot pay his moderators beyond thanks, and believes the operation should be ten times its size.
insights.speaker: Lama Rabah
insights.so_what: A critical public utility runs on unpaid labor, a sustainability and key-person risk.

insights.claim: Computer engineers Musab Nuirat and Ahmed Gharib launched the app A Ween Rayeh in 2025, a real-time traffic heat map; by Nuirat's count it was the seventh local attempt at a West Bank navigation system, and like nearly all the others it relied on Hattab's data.
insights.speaker: Lama Rabah
insights.so_what: Local app builders have repeatedly failed to build their own data layer, so the Telegram feed is the de facto platform.

insights.claim: Hattab quit his newspaper job for a construction-equipment sales role so that he would drive a different road every day, saying his point 'is not sales' but Road Conditions.
insights.speaker: Lama Rabah
insights.so_what: The founder organizes his livelihood around data collection.
